<reason>Both sides were skilled, but B won the decisive clash. A's best move—the "defaults bind everyone, no age flag needed" reframe—was genuinely clever and initially dissolved B's verification fork. But B trapped A into a real contradiction: A called universal adult ID a "strawman" in Rebuttal 1, then embraced exactly that structure (universal caps removable only by proving adulthood) in Rebuttal 2, which B skewered in the closing via the "volunteers" line against A5.4. B also neutralized A's emotional core ("the child nobody catches") by showing the account-sharing child fails under both models, a point A answered only by reassertion. B's layer argument (platforms hold the age and payment data; dev mandates add compliance surface and data copies without new protection) survived the exchange, and B's pressure questions were sharper and better exploited. A's design-harm material (pity timers, near-miss animations) went largely uncontested and kept a live route alive, as did the layered-regulation analogy, preventing a wider margin. Both closings were clipped, an equal execution cost.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 [B2.1]-[B2.2] forced the fork ("either the limits are real and every adult submits identity, or the limits are a toggle"), which A called a strawman—then B's Rebuttal 2 [B4.5] and Closing [B5.4] caught A embracing the very ID-checkpoint structure it had derided, in A's own words. That caught contradiction was the debate's turning point.</best_rebuttal>
